messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 61

# The Weight of the Kitchen

Kofi is twenty-one years old, and he has learned to keep moving. In the kitchen where he works, movement is survival — there is always a sauce to reduce, a station to clean, a ticket coming in — and for a long time he believed that if he stayed in motion long enough, what happened to him eighteen months ago might eventually fall behind.

It was at a party, late into the night, hosted by someone he considered a friend. Kofi had been drinking, though not heavily, and at some point the evening narrowed into a room he did not choose to enter and a door that closed behind him. A man he knew assaulted him. Kofi did not fight back — not because he didn't want to, but because his body simply stopped belonging to him. He lay still and waited for it to be over, and that stillness has haunted him ever since. When he thinks about that night, which is often and always uninvited, what returns most viciously is not the assault itself but the image of his own hands — open, motionless, resting at his sides as if he had simply agreed.

He told no one. In the weeks that followed, he threw himself into his culinary apprenticeship with a ferocity that impressed his head chef and worried his mother. He began arriving at the restaurant before anyone else, staying after close, scrubbing down surfaces that were already clean. The routine felt like armor. As long as he was plating, chopping, managing the controlled chaos of a dinner service, he did not have to be alone with himself.

But the kitchen has started to betray him. The walk-in refrigerator — small, cold, the door heavy — sometimes stops him completely. He will stand at the threshold for a moment too long, his chest tightening, his vision narrowing, before a colleague calls his name and pulls him back. He has never explained why. On two occasions he has had to step outside mid-service, standing in the alley behind the restaurant with his hands on his knees, breathing through something he cannot name to the people who come to check on him.

Sleep is unreliable. He falls asleep quickly, exhausted from long shifts, but wakes between two and four in the morning with his heart already racing, the sheets damp, the dream already dissolving but leaving its residue — shame, exposure, the feeling of being pinned not by force but by his own body's failure to act. He lies awake for hours, scrolling his phone, watching the ceiling, running through the night of the assault and editing it in his mind — what he should have said, what he should have done — as though if he revises it enough times it will change.

He has withdrawn from most of his friendships. His closest friend from culinary school has texted several times without response. Kofi reads the messages and means to reply, but something in the intimacy of it — being known, being asked how he is — feels dangerous in a way he cannot fully articulate. He keeps his interactions transactional: orders, deliveries, brief exchanges with colleagues about mise en place and timing. He is well-liked at work because he is competent and calm. No one suspects that calm costs him almost everything he has.

He carries a particular and corrosive belief that what happened was partly his fault — that a man his size, his age, should have been able to stop it, and that his stillness that night was a form of consent or cowardice or both. He has never framed it as assault when thinking about it privately. He calls it, in his own mind, *the thing that happened*, as if giving it a smaller name might make it take up less space. It takes up enormous space. It is in the walk-in, in the early morning hours, in his unanswered messages, in every moment he stands at a threshold deciding whether or not he can go through.
